20. FEMALE GENITAL MUTILATION (FGM):

WHO FGM Classification:

Type I: Partial/Total removal of clitoris/prepuce, clitoridectomy.

Type II: Type 1 + removal of labia minora with or without labia Majora (excision).

Type III: infibulation:

- Narrowing of vaginal orifice with creation of a covering seal by cutting and a positioning the labia minora &/or a majora with or without excision of clitoris.

Type IV: All other harmful procedure to genitalia for non-medical purposes like: pricing, pricking, incising, scraping & cauterization.

Global Epidemiology:

UNICEF: 125million all over the world.

Cultural practice in 29 countries.

Type 3 in Africa.

Done between Age of infancy & up to 15yrs.

50% below 15yrs.

137,000 women in UK have FGM.

10,000 under 15yrs.

Commonest in Somalia 98%.

Guinea 96%.

Complications of FGM:

Short term:

Hemorrhage (5 – 62%).

Urinary Retention (8 – 53%).

Genital Swelling (2 – 27%).

Fever

Infection

Long term:

Genital scarring:

Keloid 3%

Epidermoid inclusion cyst

Sebaceous cyst

Neuroma of clitoris

Urinary Track Complications:

More in Type 2 & Type 3

Urinary obstruction leads to stasis of urine(1. Recurrent Uti, 2. urinary calculi, 3. vaginal calculi)

t/m is de-infibulation.

Urinary stricture/fistula referred to urologist or urogynaecologist.

Hampers urodynamic testing.

Sexual functions:

Dyspareunia

Apareunia

Vulvovaginal lacerations

Absence of sexual sensitivity

Decreased sexual desire, Arousal and Orgasm

Decrease lubrication

Poor sexual satisfaction

Psychological:

PTSD

Anxiety

Flashbacks

Menstrual disorders:

Haematocolpus

Dysmenorrhea

C/section

Genital trauma

ENND

Still birth

Need for resuscitation.

Genital infections:

Risk of bacterial vaginosis, HSV – 2

Similar risk of chlamydia gonorrhea, syphilis, PiD

Infertility:

Primary due to sexual problems and ascending infection

Viral infections:

Hep B, C, HIV

Obstetric complications:

PPH

Prolong labor – C/section

Genital trauma

ENND

Still birth

Need for resuscitation.

FEMALE GENITAL MUTATION ACT:

FGM is illegal unless done until.

(1). For physical/Mental health of women.

(2). Purpose of labor/Birth.

FGM – arranging, facilitation and Assistance is illegal.

Offence for those with parental responsibility to fail to protect a girl from risk of FGM.

FGM in <18 years’ girl Report to police within 1 month.

Female Genital cosmetic surgery FGCS (including tightening)

Prohibited unless for physical/mental health.

Surgeons should make sure compliance with FGM act.

Infibulation is illegal – No justification.

Legal and regulatory responsibilities of health professionals:

Data recording:

Data recording is mandatory for all women identified as having FGM.

Document FGM diagnosis in medical records (even if the FGM is not the reason for presentation).

If genital examination is performed and type of FGM is identifies, record FGM type (WHO classification).

Document further details in accordance with the HSCIC FGM Enhanced Dataset.

Explain to the woman that her personal data will be transmitted to the HSCIC for the purpose of FGM prevalence monitoring and that the data will not be anonymized.

Reporting to police and/or social services in the event of risk to a child:

Children under 18:

If FGM is confirmed (on examination or if the patient or parent says it has been done). Refer as a matter of urgency to the police and this should be done within 1 month of confirmation.

If FGM is suspected (but not confirmed) or the girl is at risk (but has not had FGM), refer to social services or the police. The urgency of the referral depends on the degree of risk.

Non pregnant women with FGM: no requirement to report unless a related child is at risk.

Pregnant women:

A member of the clinical team) midwife or obstetrician) must make an individual risk assessment using an FGM safeguarding risk assessment tool ad if the unborn child, or any other child in the family, is considered to be at risk of FGM then reporting to social services or the police must occur Document maternal history of FGM in the personal child health record (‘Red book’) prior to postnatal discharge.

If delivery of a baby girl, notify the designated child protection midwife, who should inform the GP and health visitor.

>>>Genital piercing should be classified as type 4 FGM in accordance with the WHO FGM classification.

Clinical management of adult women with FGM in obstetric and gynecological practice

All acute trusts/health boards should have a designated consultant and midwife responsible for the care of women with FGM.

All women in obstetric and gynecological practice.

Explain law on FGM, documenting the discussion and referring her to information provided

Provide interpreter if required (not a family member).

Offer referral for psychological assessment and treatment.

Offer specialist referral as appropriate, e.g. sexual health, urology.

Make a clinical assessment of FGM (symptoms, examination) and need for de-infibulation.

Record data in accordance with the HSCIC FGM Enhanced Dataset. These include age at FGM, country where FGM was performed, date of entry to UK (if applicable) and past history of de-infibulation and/or re-infibulation.

If de infibulation is indicated, offer before pregnancy it can usually be performed on an outpatient basis.

ideally before 1st intercourse

Reporting to social services or the police is only required if a related child is considered to be at risk.

Additional management in pregnant women.

Refer to designated consultant obstetrician or specialist midwife with responsibility for women with FGM.

Local protocols will determine which elements of care (child safeguarding risk assessment, data recording, clinical management) should be undertaken by the designated midwife or obstetrician and which may be undertaken by other appropriately trained midwives or obstetricians.

Discuss and clearly document a plan of care, preformatted Performa’s may be used.

Make an individual risk assessment using an FGM safeguarding risk assessment tool (an example of such a tool. If the unborn child or any related child is considered to be at risk then reporting to social services or the police must occur.

All women with FGM are offered psychological assessment is t/m.

Offer screening for hepatitis C in addition to routine screening for hepatitis B, HIV and syphilis.

If de-infibulation is indicated, discuss, agree and document the timing (antenatal or intrapartum). Inform the woman that re-infibulation after delivery will not be performed under any circumstances.

Manage as high obstetric risk (increased risk of hemorrhage, perineal trauma and caesarean section), except for women who have had previous pregnancies with uncomplicated vaginal deliveries and no history of post-delivery re-infibulation.

Document maternal history of FGM in the personal child health record ('Red Book') prior to postnatal discharge.

If delivery of a baby girl, notify the designated child protection midwife, who should inform the GP and health visitor.

Offer postnatal follow-up if de-infibulation performed intrapartum or if planned de-infibulation did not occur because of delivery by caesarean section.

Indications for De-Infibulation:

Too tight introits to allow menstrual flow, vaginal examination, normal urination or comfortable sexual intercourse & safe vaginal delivery.

Before gynecological surgery, TOP, Cervix Smear, Sexual health screening.

Type III.

Plan of care for women with FGM in pregnancy:

- Document maternal history of FGM in personal child health record (Red Book').- If delivery of baby girl, notify safeguarding midwife who should inform the GP and health visitor.- Offer postnatal follow-up if de infibulation performed intrapartum er if planned de-infibulation did not occur because of delivery by caesarean section- Ensure all data required for HSCIC Enhanced Dataset have been recorded.- Generally, manage as high risk for caesarean section, hemorrhage and perineal trauma- Some women may be considered low risk and suitable for midwifery-led care if history of previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery- If de-infibulation is required, ensure that the midwife and obstetrician caring for the woman have received appropriate training- Perineal tears in women with FGM should be managed in the same manner as in women without FGM.- Use professional interpreter if required (not family member) and explain law on FGM.- Offer referral for psychological assessment and screening for hepatitis in addition to routine antenatal screening.- Make clinical assessment of FGM.
